You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

The cellular interactions that drive the neuropathology of most neuroinvasive viruses remain elusive. We used Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) to infect female BALB/c mice and apply Stereo-seq to simultaneously capture host and viral transcriptomes in situ, thereby constructing a comprehensive spatiotemporal atlas of Japanese encephalitis (JE) pathogenesis. Our analysis pinpoints Ly6c2+ monocytes as the primary virus carrier, the most abundant infiltrating immune cell type, and a major source of IFN-γ in the infected mouse brain. Following infection, Ackr1+ endothelial cell activation is linked to blood-brain barrier disruption and immune cell chemotaxis, particularly Ly6c2+ monocytes. The crosstalk between these two cell types appears to orchestrate the pronounced inflammation and cell death, including pyroptosis and necroptosis, which radiate from the vasculature to different brain regions. Disrupting the activation and interactions of these two cell types may help mitigate JE progression. This study also provides a technical framework for investigating the pathogenesis of other neurotropic viruses.

---

## Introduction

Japanese encephalitis (JE) is an acute inflammatory central nervous system (CNS) disease caused by Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV), which is primarily transmitted by the Culex mosquitos1. Local transmission of JEV occurs in 24 countries in East Asia and the Western Pacific, putting over 3 billion people at risk of infection2,3. After infection, the condition can progress to encephalitis, characterized by severe fever, neck stiffness, and seizures. Children under the age of 14 account for 75% of the JE patients3. 20-30% of JE patients die, while 30-50% of survivors develop persistent neurological or psychiatric sequelae4. Although the JEV vaccines are commercially available to reduce JE incidences5, infection risk persists for individuals lacking prior vaccinations6–8. With no virus-specific treatment available, JEV imposes a continuous burden on public health.

Following a skin bite, JEV infects susceptible myeloid immune cells, including dendritic cells, macrophages, and monocytes9–12. At the biting sites, the infected monocytic lineage cells can recirculate to the draining lymph nodes and spleen, where they undergo substantial proliferation and release progeny viruses into the lymphatic system and bloodstream, ultimately resulting in viremia13–16. A key step in JEV infection of the brain is to breach the blood-brain barrier (BBB), and the mechanisms are still debated. The BBB is composed of brain microvascular endothelial cells (BMECs), tight junctions between endothelial cells, the basement membrane, and astrocytic end-feet. It plays a crucial role in maintaining the homeostasis of the brain's internal environment. Some studies suggest that JEV can directly infect BMECs, which subsequently release progeny viruses from the basal side into the brain parenchyma17. Other studies propose that early JEV-induced inflammatory factors affect BMECs by downregulating tight junctions, thus increasing BBB permeability and facilitating viral entry into the brain18,19. Additionally, the virus can infect immune cells (such as macrophages and monocytes), which are then able to cross the damaged BBB and unintentionally transport the virus into the brain, much like the Greek "Trojan Horse", where something harmful is smuggled inside something that appears harmless20. Nevertheless, considerable controversy remains regarding the specific cell types and pathways mediating viral entry into the brain parenchyma.

JEV can infect many brain parenchymal regions such as thalamus, brainstem, and hippocampus21,22. The replication of JEV in neurons can lead to direct neuronal death, while the activated microglia/glial cells and infiltrating inflammatory cells can also damage or kill the neurons by releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF-α as well as other cytotoxic factors23,24. Studies have identified monocytes as an essential cell type contributing to JE neuropathology25–27. Inflammatory Ly6chi monocytes have paradoxical roles in viral encephalitis. On one hand, monocytes can differentiate into effector cells and produce reactive oxygen species (ROS) which repress and clear the virus. On the other hand, unbalanced and uncontrolled migration and infiltration of monocytes will facilitate viral neuroinvasion through a "Trojan horse" manner and cause excessive tissue damage28–30. At present, the specific mechanisms underlying monocyte infiltration into brain tissue and their overall contribution to the pathogenesis of encephalitis remain unclear, warranting further in-depth investigation.

As key constituents of the brain’s barriers, the meninges and choroid plexus can serve as gateways for the entry of various neuroinvasive pathogens such as JEV, mediate the infiltration of myeloid immune cells, and participate in orchestrating immune response in the CNS19,31–34. These processes all depend on the engagement of endothelial cells. It is also reported that human brain microvascular endothelial cells (HBMEC) can support JEV replication and promote leukocyte adhesion in vitro17,35. However, there exists a lack of understanding of the in situ interaction networks between the endothelial cells and infiltrating immune cell types within the brain following JEV infection. Moreover, the precise cellular changes associated with JEV-induced tissue damage in the CNS remain largely elusive. Therefore, an integrated and systematic analysis of JE pathogenesis is urgently needed.

Recent investigations into the pathogenesis of neurotropic viruses have been advanced by single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), which elucidates the immune functions of microglia, monocytes, and other immune cells in the cerebrospinal fluid and brain tissues24,36–38. However, scRNA-seq requires tissue dissociation, a process that can lead to the loss of low-viability cells and poses significant challenges for the effective isolation of neurons. Consequently, this approach may fail to provide a complete picture of brain pathology. In contrast, spatial transcriptomics can capture transcripts in situ within intact tissue architectures. This technology can therefore elucidate the regional tropism of viral infection, the spatial infiltration patterns of immune cells, the extent of infiltration by various immune subsets, the degree of tissue damage, and the neighborhood interactions between different cell types, providing high-resolution molecular evidence for deciphering the pathogenic mechanisms of neuroinvasive viruses39.

In this study, we construct a female BALB/c mouse infection model and design Stereo-seq chips with JEV probes that can simultaneously detect JEV and host transcriptomes to dissect the spatial and temporal transcriptional features of neurological lesions during JEV acute infection phase, identify the key cells, pathways, and inflammatory factors associated with brain damage, providing clues on the diagnosis and treatment of JE. As a member of the Orthoflavivirus genus, JEV characteristically lacks a polyA tail, posing a detection hurdle for mRNA capture methods, including scRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics technologies, that predominantly utilize polyT probes40. This work establishes a spatial transcriptomics technical framework that can be adapted to study the immunology of other orthoflaviviruses and neuroinvasive viruses, which will benefit the mechanistic exploration and the discovery of novel therapeutic targets in associated diseases.

---

## Results

Custom Stereo-seq chips reveal the spatial profiles of JEV infection. To explore JEV infection dynamics in the mouse brain, we inoculated female BALB/c mice with 106 PFU of JEV in 200 μl of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) or 200 μl of PBS in the mock-treated group (Fig. 1a). On the 3rd, 5th, and 7th day post inoculation (dpi), the mouse brains (n=3) were collected for Stereo-seq experiment (Fig. 1a). The selection of these time points was based on key experimental observations as described in methods and shown in the supplementary information (Supplementary Fig. 1a-f): 3 dpi corresponded to the peak of viremia and the initial detection of JEV RNA in the brain (marking viral entry into the CNS); 5 dpi fell in the active phase of intracerebral viral replication and early disease progression (after the onset of clinical signs on 4 dpi); and 7 dpi represented the pre-mortality window (prior to the onset of mortality on 8 dpi) with escalating clinical symptoms and sustained high intracerebral viral load. These time points ensured the capture of critical stages of JEV acute infection. The original Stereo-seq technology utilizes polyT probes to capture mRNA41. However, the mRNA of JEV lacks a polyA tail, which cannot be readily detected. To facilitate the capture of JEV transcripts, we strategically designed a virus-specific probe (VSP) targeting a conserved region in the NS5 gene of multiple orthoflaviviruses (including JEV, Zika virus, and Dengue virus). The VSPs were integrated into the existing polyT probes at a ratio of 1:10 on the Stereo-seq chips (Fig. 1a). Based on our preliminary solution-phase test, this ratio enabled more sensitive detection of JEV than random primers, without compromising the detection of host transcripts. Data from Stereo-seq experiments using JEV-infected mouse brain tissues showed that the captured reads were mainly attributable to polyT and VSPs, with polyT probes capturing approximately 70% of the overall reads, mostly mouse transcripts (Supplementary Fig. 1g). When it comes to the detection of JEV transcripts, the VSPs captured over 80% of the reads (Supplementary Fig. 1g). During viral replication, JEV expresses only a single genomic RNA that serves as mRNA and does not generate multiple distinct transcripts. When quantifying JEV expression, we assumed that each detected viral RNA fragment corresponds to an intact JEV RNA. Although VSPs were included in the chips, the total number of probes that can be anchored on each spot is limited and that the probe density in certain capture spots may be lower than the actual number of viral mRNAs present in the tissue. In addition, steric hindrance may prevent a virus-targeted probe from hybridizing to its cognate mRNA. Consequently, our spatial transcriptomic data provide a qualitative map of JEV distribution rather than an absolute quantification of viral load within each region.

Based on the overall data quality, we chose an analytical unit of bin35, representing a square region of 35 spots x 35 spots, equal to 17.22 μm x 17.22 μm. The median number of genes detected for each bin ranged from 396 to 844, with an average of 671 genes (Supplementary Data 1). The spatial transcriptomics data showed that the JEV genes were expressed in approximately 0.04%, 3.49%, and 4.25% area of the brain tissues on 3, 5, and 7 dpi respectively, reaching a peak on 7 dpi; while no JEV-positive bins were identified in the control samples (Supplementary Data 1). These results were consistent with the JEV load detected by reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) (Supplementary Fig. 1b), confirming the reliability of the spatial transcriptomic data. To determine the specific regions infected by JEV, we annotated the mouse brain regions using the marker genes and anatomical information from the Allen Brain Atlas (https://atlas.brain-map.org/, Supplementary Data 2). For instance, the thalamus was annotated using marker genes such as Prkcd, Tcf7l2, and Ntng1, while the meninges were annotated by genes such as Tmem212, Igfbp4, Ccdc153, and Ptgds. Our data showed that the thalamus, cerebral cortex, and cerebral nuclei were the most infected regions by JEV (Supplementary Data 3, Fig. 1b,c), consistent with previous reports22,42. On 3 dpi, most brain regions were negative for JEV infection. On 5 dpi, multiple brain regions were JEV positive, but the percentages of virus positive bins in thalamus, cerebral cortex, and cerebral nuclei were less than 20%. On 7 dpi, the JEV positive rates in these brain regions rose to 20%-40%, indicating continuous amplification of JEV in these sites.

We further employed SingleR43 and its accompanying reference dataset to annotate the cell types (Supplementary Fig. 2a, Supplementary Data 4) and characterized the cellular infection profiles (Supplementary Data 5&6). On 3 dpi, monocytes were the dominant JEV positive cells, with an average positive rate of 0.93% (Fig. 1d). On 5 dpi, the highest JEV positive rate was observed in NK cells, 9.65%, followed by dendritic cells (6.12%), microglia (5.25%), macrophages (4.60%), and neurons (3.79%). On 7 dpi, the highest JEV positive rate was observed in microglia (7.60%), followed by NK cells (6.73%). The virus positive rates of NK cells and dendritic cells reached an early peak on 5 dpi. In contrast, the rates in the other cell types showed a rising trend from 3 to 7 dpi, including microglia, macrophages, neurons, T cells, fibroblasts, monocytes, granulocytes, endothelial cells, epithelial cells, and astrocytes (Fig. 1d). Among them, most were brain-resident cells, indicating progressive replication of JEV in the brain parenchyma. Our data suggests that monocytes may be the initial infected cells in the CNS and further spread the virus to the resident cell types in the brain. The phagocytosis of JEV-infected cells and natural viral infection may collectively contribute to the high positive rates of multiple immune cells.

We next verified the high infection rates of immune cells in the brain using flow cytometry. When considering the percentage of JEV-infected cells within each immune cell type (Supplementary Fig. 2b-e, upper panel), macrophages (16.8% infection rate at 5 dpi) and NK cells (15.4% infection rate at 7 dpi) exhibited the highest JEV infection rates among all infiltrating immune cells in the brain. However, when assessing the proportion of JEV-infected immune cells relative to the total brain cells (Supplementary Fig. 2b-e, lower panel), which better reflected the overall contribution of specific immune cell types to the brain infection, JEV+ monocytes were the predominant infected immune cells, accounting for around 0.08% of the total living cells in the brain at 5 dpi. This evidence indicates that monocytes may be the key immune cell type mediating JEV infection in the brain.

Spatiotemporal immunological landscape during JE progression. To gain a comprehensive view of the cerebral immunological and physiological alterations following JEV infection, we conducted a comparative analysis to identify the temporal transcriptional changes. A total of 225 genes were differentially expressed between the infection and control groups (Supplementary Data 7). Chronologically, 35, 203, and 112 genes were upregulated on 3, 5, and 7 dpi, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 3a), with 95 genes upregulated on both 5 dpi and 7 dpi. Meanwhile, a total of 58 genes were downregulated after infection, with 2, 6, and 56 genes downregulated on 3, 5, and 7 dpi, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 3b). Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis revealed that the upregulated genes in JEV infection groups were mainly associated with immune response (Supplementary Fig. 3c), while the downregulated genes were mostly associated with functional pathways of brain cells including exocytosis, synapse organization, and neurotransmitter transport, indicating functional damage in the brain (Supplementary Fig. 3d). Starting from 3 dpi, innate immune response was initiated to recruit lymphocytes, produce interferons and cytokines, induce cell killing, and inhibit virus replication. We observed an early activation of type I interferons (IFN-α and IFN-β) starting from 3 dpi, followed by the activation of type II interferon (IFN-γ) on 5 dpi (Supplementary Fig. 3c). Stimulated by virus infection, expression levels of multiple Toll-like receptors were enhanced since 3 dpi (Supplementary Fig. 3e), especially Tlr8, Tlr2, Tlr3 and Tlr7. A series of interferon regulatory factors (IRFs) were also upregulated (Supplementary Fig. 3f), such as Irf7, Irf1, Irf8, Irf9, Irf5, and Irf4. The expression of these genes mostly peaked on 5 dpi. Consistently, most of the interferon genes were initially expressed on 3 dpi, peaked on 5 dpi, and were downregulated on 7 dpi (Supplementary Fig. 4a). Consequently, the interferon-inducible genes showed low expression levels on 3 dpi but higher levels on 5 dpi and 7 dpi (Supplementary Fig. 4b). The expressions of representative Tlr, Irf, and Ifn genes were further validated by RT-qPCR (Supplementary Fig. 4c). On 5 dpi, the pathways including Toll-like receptor signaling, ribosome assembly, protein folding, and cytoplasmic translation were uniquely upregulated (Supplementary Fig. 3c), which may be linked to the active replication of JEV in the brain. More immune cell types were activated on 5 dpi, including astrocyte development, glial cell differentiation and migration, chemotaxis of granulocytes and lymphocytes (Supplementary Fig. 3c). On 7 dpi, the immune response was further strengthened by B cell mediated immunity and the activation of myeloid leukocytes and macrophages (Supplementary Fig. 3c).

Spatial mapping of the upregulated immune genes such as Irf7, Ifng, Ifitm3, Isg15, Cxcl10, and Ccl2 revealed significantly high expression levels along the vasculatures in the brain (Fig. 2a). To understand the immune response status of different brain regions, we conducted Gene Set Variation Analysis (GSVA) for each brain sample based on the pro-inflammatory gene set from the GSEA database44–46 (Supplementary Data 8). Our data showed that the meninges and choroid plexus had the highest immune response scores across different infection timepoints, followed by the brain regions with high infection rates such as the thalamus and cerebral cortex (Fig. 2b), especially on 5 and 7 dpi. Immunofluorescent staining revealed enhanced expression of CXCL10, CXCL9, and CCL2 in the meninges (Fig. 2c-e). Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining showed that vascular dilation in the meningeal tissues began at 3 dpi, accompanied by the adhesion of inflammatory cells to the vascular endothelium. At 5 and 7 dpi, vascular dilation became more pronounced, with a significant increase in the number of adherent inflammatory cells (Fig. 2f). The inflammatory response initiated at 3 dpi, peaked at 5 dpi, and decreased at 7 dpi, but still remained higher than that of 3 dpi (Fig. 2b). These observations demonstrate that the cerebral vasculatures, particularly those in the meninges, is involved from the early stages during the inflammatory progression of JE.

At cellular level, comparative temporal analysis of whole Stereo-seq chips demonstrated an increase in the numbers of monocytes, macrophages, T cells, and microglia, in contrast to a progressive decline in the number of neurons (Fig. 3a). We also observed increased signals of endothelial cells, which was probably due to vascular dilation caused by immune infiltration or tissue edema (Fig. 2f), instead of cell proliferation. Flow cytometry results showed that monocytes and T cells were the major immune cells infiltrating into the JEV-infected brain (Fig. 3b). Remarkably, monocytes accounted for over 0.6% of the living cells in the infected brain at 7 dpi (Fig. 3b), potentially dominating the immune response against JEV infection.

IFN-γ is a critical immunomodulatory cytokine that coordinates both innate and adaptive immune responses and also exerts powerful antiviral function47. Studies have also shown that IFN-γ is a key cytokine mediating BBB disruption and immune cell infiltration in the pathogenesis of JE48,49. Therefore, identifying the specific cell types in the brain that secrete IFN-γ would help reveal the drivers of JE immunopathology. To validate the cellular sources of IFN-γ in the JEV-infected mouse brain, we performed flow cytometric analysis. The number of IFN-γ-producing cells increased at 5 and 7 dpi, despite representing only approximately 1% of the total brain cells (Fig. 3c). Notably, at 5 and 7 dpi, when cerebral viral loads were high, immune cells constituted up to 50% of all IFN-γ-producing cells (Fig. 3d). Within the IFN-γ⁺CD45⁺ cell population, T cells accounted for 3.6–5.0% (Fig. 3e), NK cells for 6.3–6.9% (Fig. 3f), and macrophages for 2.5–5.5% (Fig. 3g). Strikingly, monocytes represented the majority, comprising 28.3% and 25.6% of the IFN-γ-producing immune cells at 5 and 7 dpi, respectively (Fig. 3h), suggesting monocytes as the principal source of IFN-γ in the brain during JE.

It is widely recognized that activated T cells and NK cells are the primary sources of IFN-γ, whereas monocytes are generally not considered IFN-γ producers. However, several studies have reported that, under specific stimulatory conditions, monocytes are capable of secreting IFN-γ and may even represent a major source50,51. To further corroborate our transcriptomic and flow cytometry findings, we isolated monocytes from both mouse and human peripheral blood and infected them with JEV in vitro. Compared to uninfected controls, JEV-infected monocytes exhibited significantly increased cellular IFN-γ mRNA and extracellular protein expressions (Fig. 3i-l). These results confirm infiltrating monocytes as a major source of IFN-γ in the brain during JE. Given that the majority of infected mice ultimately succumbed to death (Supplementary Fig. 1e), these IFN-γ-secreting monocytes might contribute to disease exacerbation.

Activation and pro-inflammatory function of Ackr1+ endothelial cells. Our results showed that the meninges were the hotspot of immune response, and the excessive immune infiltration also caused tissue damage (Fig. 2). To further understand the transcriptional changes associated with this pathological process, we extracted the spatial transcriptomics data of meninges from all samples for in-depth investigation. Analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) showed that many inflammatory molecules including Cxcl10 and Ccl2, as well as MHCII-related genes (B2m and H2-K1) were upregulated in samples collected on 5 and 7 dpi (Supplementary Fig. 5a). We further conducted cell clustering and annotations using the bin35 data of meninges (Supplementary Fig. 5b,c). By sub-clustering the Ly6c2+ cells, we identified a cluster of brain endothelial cells (ECs) highly expressing Ackr1 (atypical chemokine receptor 1), defined as Ackr1+ ECs (Fig. 4a). The Ackr1+ ECs highly expressed marker genes that were enriched in angiogenesis and vascular pathways52 (Supplementary Fig. 5d), including Vwf and Igfbp7 (Fig. 4b). Sequential comparative analysis showed an increase in the proportion of Ackr1+ ECs after infection, especially on 5 and 7 dpi, along with significant infiltration of Ly6c2+Lyz2+ monocytes into the meninges on 5 dpi (Fig. 4c). Cell-cell communication53 analysis of the meninges revealed strong interactions between Ackr1+ ECs and Ly6c2+Lyz2+ monocytes via the CCL/CXCL pathway (Fig. 4d,e,f), which was significantly upregulated on 5 dpi and 7 dpi (Fig. 4d). The Ackr1+ ECs may recruit Ly6c2+Lyz2+ monocytes highly expressing Cxcl9, Cxcl10, Ccl7, Ccl5 and Ccl2 (Supplementary Fig. 6a). Moreover, the Ly6c2+Lyz2+ monocytes also expressed a high level of Ackr1, Ccr2, Ccr1, and Ccr5, which may further facilitate the recruitment of monocytes and T cells (Supplementary Fig. 6a). Spatial transcriptomic data displayed strong co-localization signals for ligand-receptor pairs including Ccl7-Ccr2, Ccl2-Ccr2, Ccl5-Ccr1, Ccl2-Ccr5 and Cxcl9/Cxcl10/Ccl7/Ccl5/Ccl2-Ackr1 in the meningeal region on 5 and 7 dpi (Fig. 4g). Further in situ immunofluorescent staining showed increased protein expression levels of ACKR1, CXCL10, CXCL9, and CCL2 in the meninges following JEV infection (Fig. 4h, Supplementary Fig. 6b,c). Notably, cells positive for CXCL10, CXCL9, or CCL2 were situated in close proximity to Ackr1-expressing cells, confirming interactions between Ackr1+ ECs and inflammatory cells. Regulatory factor analysis54 with the cytokines expressed by Ly6c2+Lyz2+ monocytes revealed that the downstream target genes in Ackr1+ ECs included Ccl12, Ccl4, Ccl7, and Ptgs2 (Fig. 4i), which can further promote the production of proinflammatory cytokines by Ackr1+ ECs (Fig. 4j).

Disruption of the BBB is crucial for immune cell infiltration and virus invasion into the brain. On 5 and 7 dpi, the tight junction associated genes such as Tjp1 and Cldn5 were downregulated (Fig. 5a), which was further validated by immunofluorescent staining (Fig. 5b,c), suggesting the impairment of the BBB. To further assess changes in BBB permeability following JEV infection, we employed the widely used Evans blue assay. The results demonstrated a significant increase in BBB permeability at 5 and 7 dpi (Fig. 5d), indicating that JEV infection markedly disrupts BBB integrity. Moreover, spatial transcriptomics data, immunofluorescent staining and RT-qPCR results demonstrated that the expressions of Ackr1 (Fig. 5a,e) as well as adhesion molecule genes Icam1 (Fig. 5a,e,f), and Vcam1 (Fig. 5a,g,h) were upregulated on 5 and 7 dpi in the meninges, which may promote the transendothelial migration of monocytes and other immune cells28. Notably, besides a small number of viral RNA detected in the ECs (Fig. 1d), we also observed the upregulation of a series of pattern recognition receptors55–57 (PRRs) in different types of ECs, including Tlr1, Tlr2, Tlr3, Tlr4, Tlr6, Tlr7, Tlr13, Ifih1, and Ddx58, suggesting potential JEV infection in the ECs (Fig. 5i). The ECs also displayed higher interferon production activities, as the gene expressions of interferon regulatory factors (Stat3, Stat2, Stat1, Irf7, and Cebpd) and interferon receptors (Ifnar2, Ifngr2), were also upregulated in these cells (Fig. 5i).

To obtain single-cell resolution evidence, we performed cell segmentation on mouse brains collected from the control (n=2) and 5 dpi (n=1) groups and extracted the segmented cells in the meningeal region. Similar to the results based on bin35 data, Ackr1+ ECs were identified in the meningeal region collected on 5 dpi (Supplementary Fig. 7a-c). Regulatory analysis with Pyscenic58 showed that Ackr1+ ECs exhibited activation of a series of specific transcription factors (Supplementary Fig. 7d), among which Irf7, Stat1, Cebpb, Cebpd, Spi1, and Irf1 were highly expressed in the Ackr1+ ECs (Supplementary Fig. 7e), with Irf7 displaying the highest expression level. Cell-cell communication analysis with the segmented cell data further confirmed the interactions between Ackr1+ ECs and Ly6c2+Lyz2+ monocytes through the Cxcl10/Ccl2/Ccl5/Cc7-Ackr1 axes (Supplementary Fig. 7f,g). Remarkably, the single-cell resolution data showed that among the three types of ECs, Ackr1+ ECs significantly upregulated the expression of genes associated with pathogen recognition, interferon production, and cell adhesion (Supplementary Fig. 7h,i). These results reveal the central role of Ackr1+ ECs in receiving and amplifying immune signals during the progression of JE.

Activation and expansion of Ccl12+ microglia. Microglia account for approximately 5%-20% of the total glia cell population and are vital to pathogen defense in the brain59. Indeed, we observed a sharp increase of activated microglia in the mouse brain after JEV infection (Fig. 6a). By examining the expression of pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory markers, we observed increased expressions of pro-inflammatory genes including Cd14, Fcgr3, Fcgr2b, Cd40, Cd86, and H2-Ab1 in the microglia, particularly on 5 and 7 dpi (Supplementary Fig. 8a,b). Pro-inflammatory chemokines such as Ccl3, Ccl4, Ccl5, and Ccl12 were also significantly upregulated in microglia on 5 and 7 dpi (Supplementary Fig. 8a), suggesting microglia activation. Ccl12 was specifically expressed in the activated microglia but not in the homeostatic ones (Fig. 6a,b). Therefore, we defined the activated microglia as Ccl12+ microglia. The Ccl12+ microglia were mainly identified in the JEV infection groups, with few homeostatic microglia detected on 5 and 7 dpi (Fig. 6c). RT-qPCR experiment confirmed elevated expressions of Iba1 and Ccl12 (Fig. 6d,e) in the infected mouse brains while immunofluorescent staining revealed co-localization of the corresponding proteins (Fig. 6f). The presence of Ccl12+ microglia was further confirmed by an external scRNA-seq dataset (GSE237915)24 where these cells were also identified and showed a strong correlation with those in our spatial transcriptomics dataset (Supplementary Fig. 8c-e). We further conducted functional enrichment of the DEGs between Ccl12+ microglia and homeostatic microglia. The upregulated genes in Ccl12+ microglia were associated with antiviral response and interferon signaling (Fig. 6g), while the downregulated genes were linked to synapse organization, learning or memory, and cognitive pathway (Fig. 6h). This suggests that Ccl12+ microglia play a role in antiviral responses, but their transcriptional changes are linked to neuropathology. Transcriptional regulation analysis58 showed that transcriptional regulators including Irf7, Stat1, and Cebpd were active in Ccl12+ microglia (Fig. 6i), suggesting their involvement in microglia differentiation. Spatially, the expression of Irf7 not only colocalized with Ccl12+ microglia but also overlapped with Cxcl10 and the meninges (Fig. 6j), indicating a close interplay between immune cell chemotaxis and microglia activation.

Enhanced necroptosis and pyroptosis in the meninges. To understand the cell death mechanism engaged in JE progression, we estimated the transcriptional score of six death pathways including apoptosis, necroptosis, ferroptosis, cuproptosis, pyroptosis, and autophagy (Supplementary Data 8). Enhanced RNA signals were observed for necroptosis and pyroptosis during JEV infection. Genes related to necroptosis and pyroptosis were significantly upregulated in brains collected on 5 and 7 dpi (Fig. 7a,b). The RNA signals of necroptosis and pyroptosis were mainly concentrated in the meningeal regions (Fig. 7c,d), which was further confirmed by in situ immunofluorescent staining and RT-qPCR using the necroptosis marker p-MLKL (encoded by Mlkl, Fig. 7e,f) and the pyroptosis marker GSDMD-N (encoded by Gsdmd, Fig. 7g,h). Multiple cell types upregulated necroptosis and pyroptosis signals including Ackr1+ ECs, CD8+ T cells, Gfap+CD74+ astrocytes, Ly6c2+Lyz2+ monocytes, Ly6c2+Ptgds+ cells, neutrophils, and Saa+ cells (Fig. 7i,j), with Ly6c2+Lyz2+ monocytes infiltrating from the periphery exhibiting the strongest signals, which were further validated by in situ immunofluorescent co-staining of Ly6c2 and necroptosis biomarker p-MLKL (Fig. 7k) or pyroptosis marker GSDMD-N (Fig. 7l). These data demonstrate that meninges were the hotspot of necroptosis and pyroptosis and that Ly6c2+ monocytes were deeply involved in the cell death across multiple brain regions. The release of cellular contents due to necroptosis and pyroptosis could enhance the immune cascade reaction, exacerbating neuroinflammation and tissue damage.

JEV infection induces necroptosis and pyroptosis in neurons. We further focused on the brain regions with a high viral load including the thalamus, cerebral cortex, cerebral nuclei, and hindbrain, to investigate the impact of viral infection on the death of neurons in these regions (Stereo-seq bin35 data). We performed GSVA to evaluate the cell death scores between virus-positive and virus-negative neurons. To avoid potential false positive bins, only bins containing at least two different viral genes or three viral reads were defined as JEV positive. In the thalamus, the JEV-positive Meg3+ Neurons, Oxt+ Neurons, and Tac2+ Neurons exhibited higher pyroptosis and necroptosis signals than their JEV-negative counterparts (Fig. 8a,b). Consistently, genes related to necroptosis (Ripk3, Ripk1, Mlkl, Ripk2, Tnfrsf1a, and Tnf) and pyroptosis (Casp1, Casp4, Casp8, Casp9, and Gsdmd) showed upregulation in the JEV-infected Oxt+ Neurons and Tac2+ Neurons (Fig. 8c). Similarly, Meg3+ Neurons and Pvalb+ Neurons in the cerebral cortex (Supplementary Fig. 9a-f), Oxt+ Neurons and Sst+ Neurons in the cerebral nuclei (Supplementary Fig. 9g-l), as well as Gpr88+ Neurons, Vsnl1+ Neurons and Sncg+Nefl+ Neurons in the hindbrain (Supplementary Fig. 9m-r) all upregulated necroptosis and pyroptosis signals in the virus-positive cells. These results suggest that JEV infection causes loss of neurons through pyroptosis and necroptosis. Although the JEV-negative neurons had lower death signals, the uninfected neurons may also be killed by the bystander effect. Unfortunately, because our virus probes may be insufficient to capture all JEV RNA in each cell, a JEV-negative cell may be JEV-infected, making it hard to define a true bystander cell. Therefore, our detection sensitivity can't support the discrimination between direct virus-induced and bystander cell death. Meanwhile, the necroptosis and pyroptosis signals in the immune cells were upregulated independent of virus infection (Fig. 8b,c and Supplementary Fig. 9d-f,j-l,p-r), suggesting a more complex cell death mechanism of the infiltrating immune cells.

Genes associated with JE neurological disorders. JE patients may experience symptoms such as confusion, aphasia, and paralysis, and the underlying mechanism was not fully explained. While DEG analysis can identify lists of individually altered genes, we would like to find out coordinately expressed gene modules associated with the neurological disorders caused by JEV infection. To achieve this, we used hdWGCNA (high-dimensional Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis) to detect the corresponding functional programs in specific cell types60. We identified modules related to learning, memory, and cognition in multiple brain regions in response to JEV infection, including thalamus, cerebral cortex, cerebral nuclei, and hindbrain. The functional modules related to learning, memory, and cognition were significantly correlated with specific neuron subtypes, which included the Meg3+ Neurons in the thalamus (Module SM4, Fig. 9a, Supplementary Fig. 10a-c), the Meg3+ Neurons in the cerebral cortex (Module SM3, Supplementary Fig. 10d-f), the Tac1+ Neurons in the cerebral nuclei (Module SM3, Supplementary Fig. 10g-i), and the Gpr88+ Neurons in the hindbrain (Module SM6, Supplementary Fig. 10j-l). While the above-mentioned cell types tended to be systemically damaged, the other neurons may also be affected, as the individual functional genes related to learning, memory, cognition, or locomotion were downregulated in various neuron subtypes after JEV infection (Fig. 9b, Supplementary Fig. 11a-c). For instance, Ctnx3+ cells, Meg3+ Neurons, and Oxt+ Neurons of the thalamus all downregulated genes including Gnas, Cck, Snap25, and Atp1a3 (Fig. 9b). Comparative analysis revealed that 21 downregulated genes were shared by the learning, memory, and cognition pathways regardless of brain regions (Fig. 9c). Eleven genes of the learning or memory pathway were downregulated in the virus-positive cells in at least three brain regions, with Atp1a3 and Ndrg4 identified in six regions (Fig. 9d). Meanwhile, ten genes of the locomotory behavior pathway were downregulated in the virus-positive neurons in at least three brain regions, with Atp1a3 and Kcnd2 identified in six regions (Fig. 9e). In summary, JEV infection causes extensive neurological disorders through disrupting the expression of functional genes in the neurons.

Predicted Interactions between JEV and host factors. With both virus and host transcriptome detected, we sought to explore JEV and host interactions through integrative analysis. Currently, there exist few systematic studies on the protein-protein interactions (PPIs) between JEV and its host, including experimental or computational prediction. We employed an unsupervised sequence embedding method (doc2vec) and random forest classifier to identify potential PPIs between JEV and human61. A total of 588 human proteins interacting with the virus were predicted (Supplementary Data 9). There were 550 proteins that may interact with NS5 and 490 with NS3 (Supplementary Fig. 12a). By performing pathway enrichment analysis on the host proteins interacting with each viral protein, we found that each viral protein may uniquely perturb 2-7 pathways except for C protein whose interacted host proteins always overlapped with those of the other viral proteins (Supplementary Fig. 12b). The NS5 protein affects pathways related to protein stability and cell cycle mitosis, while NS3 specifically hijacks pathways related to endoplasmic reticulum processing of proteins (Supplementary Fig. 12b). The pathways commonly associated with at least seven virus proteins included antiviral response of interferon-stimulated genes, protein localization to organelles, virus infection, and RNA metabolism. Pathway enrichment of the host proteins potentially interacting with all the virus proteins revealed pathways including response to infections, cellular response to interleukin-4, rhythmic process, and HDAC6 interactions in the CNS (Supplementary Fig. 12c, Supplementary Data 10). Among them, the HDAC6 interaction and Parkin ubiquitin proteasome pathway may be involved in nervous system dysfunction. In the Parkin ubiquitin proteasome pathway, members of the HSP70, Tubulin, and 26S ubiquitin proteasome families were predicted to interact extensively with viral proteins.

Because the PPI network was predicted based on genomic data, we wished to test at the transcriptome level, whether the predicted interactions are accompanied by measurable changes in gene expression. We explored two potential strategies: 1) For genes directly implicated in PPI, we asked whether their own transcripts are significantly up- or down-regulated. 2) For genes that act indirectly, we examined the expression of their downstream targets. We first combined PPI results with our spatial transcriptomics data to identify transcriptional changes due to direct virus-host interaction. Because of the low detection level of JEV mRNAs in the spatial transcriptomic data (Supplementary Data 1), the correlation coefficients between host and viral genes were smaller than 0.25 (Supplementary Fig. 13a). Even using a low threshold (|correlation coefficient| >0.2), less than 70 host genes were found to be correlated with virus gene expression in a defined cell type and only 1-3 genes identified in the PPI were included (Supplementary Fig. 13b). When we used the segmented cell data of Sample D5_1, the number of host genes identified in a single cell type correlated with virus replication increased (|correlation coefficient| >0.2) but the overlap with PPI remained minimal (Supplementary Fig. 13c). Similar results were obtained when we conducted correlation analysis (|correlation coefficient| >0.3) using the external scRNA-seq data (GSE237915)24, although the number of overlapped genes increased (Supplementary Fig. 13d,e). Unfortunately, no genes were consistently identified across the three datasets.

While the low capture rate of mRNAs due to technical limitations may mask transcriptomic changes, it’s also possible that the viral proteins may hijack host transcription factors to influence downstream mRNA expression indirectly. For instance, the NS5 protein of Dengue virus can bind the PAF1C complex, thereby affecting the expression of downstream interferon-related genes62. Therefore, we intersected the PPI results with known transcription factors, revealing 59 transcription factors that interact with JEV proteins (Supplementary Fig. 13f) along with their downstream target genes. Because the thalamus has the highest virus infection rate among different brain regions, we decided to conduct host-virus interaction analysis using cells of the thalamus. Based on the bin35 data of the thalamus, 18 target genes correlated with viral gene expressions were identified (Supplementary Fig. 13g, Supplementary Data 11), which were regulated by 13 transcription factors. A total of 158 target genes with expression correlated with viral genes were identified in the external scRNA-seq dataset (GSE237915)24, regulated by 20 transcription factors (Supplementary Fig. 13g, Supplementary Data 11). There were 13 transcription factors and 14 target genes shared by these two datasets (Supplementary Fig. 13g), with NS3 and NS5A interacting with nearly all these 13 transcription factors (Fig. 10a). The regulatory network revealed Nfkb1, Sp1, Stat1, and Stat3 as hub transcription factors and Cdkn1a, Mt1, and Cxcl10 as hub target genes (Fig. 10b). The 14 common target genes were enriched in pathways that positively regulate monocyte chemotaxis and spinal cord injury, among which Cxcl10, Gfap, Ccl2, Mbp, and Tspo are common to both pathways (Fig. 10c). Cxcl10, Gfap, Ccl2, and Tspo showed a positive correlation with viral gene expression (Fig. 10d, Supplementary Fig. 14a), while Mbp displayed a negative correlation (Supplementary Fig. 14a). We further assessed the mRNA expression levels of Gfap, Tspo, and Mbp by RT-qPCR. The expression of Gfap and Tspo began to increase at 3 dpi, reached a peak at 5 dpi, and then slightly decreased at 7 dpi, although levels remained higher than those observed at 3 dpi (Supplementary Fig. 14b,c). In contrast, the expression of Mbp exhibited a continuous decline following JEV infection (Supplementary Fig. 14d). These results strongly suggest that the neuronal death might result in a loss of myelin basic protein (MBP) and cause potential demyelination and gliosis. Luxol Fast Blue (LFB)-Eosin staining of the myelin sheaths showed that the blue staining of myelin in JEV mouse brains collected on 5 and 7 dpi was noticeably reduced, indicating significant myelin loss (Supplementary Fig. 14e). The above results predict key molecules involved in the host response to JEV infection.

Ly6c2+ monocytes and Ackr1+ endothelial cells synergize to fuel JE. Our data suggest a central role of JEV-infected Ly6c2+ monocytes in spreading the virus to the CNS and initiating encephalitis (Fig. 10e). In addition to being the primary viral carriers into the CNS, these cells represent the predominant immune population in the infected brain, where they secrete abundant inflammatory mediators like IFN-γ, orchestrating neuroinflammation and modulating cell deaths, particularly pyroptosis. The vascular network, especially those associated with the meninges and choroid plexus, is distributed throughout the brain, where it normally shields neural tissue and delivers nutrients. Upon infection, this same network is converted into a sensor and amplifier of immune signals: Ackr1+ endothelial cells become inflamed, BBB permeability increases, and both virus and immune mediators disseminate more freely. Intense immune cell infiltration and cell damage follows; once vessels are injured, nutrient transport is impaired and post-acute repair is dampened, culminating in severe neurological deficits and death. During JE development, the interplay between Ly6c2+ monocytes and Ackr1+ endothelial cells plays a dual role, mediating host defense against viral infection while simultaneously driving tissue destruction. The resolution of inflammation targeting these two cell types within the vascular system may be essential in mitigating JE progression.
